draft.why_angle: The FranklinWH pages that rank for this search say a portable or standby generator will work. None of them gives a voltage, a start-wire type, a charge rate or an adapter limit. This page shows that generator voltage and the link to the hub decide everything. On the Anker SOLIX E10, a 120 V generator charges at 1,800 W, against 4,500 W over the Smart Generator 5500's DC cable and 7,680 W at 240 V. Auto-start needs Two Wire or Utility Sensing control, and Anker's AC Generator Adapter is 'Currently not compatible with Power Dock'.

page.after:
What the differences mean

All four kits use the same E10 inverter and the same 6.144 kWh B6000 battery modules. They differ in battery count, in how the generator reaches the battery, and in how the house is wired.

  • Refill time on the Smart Generator 5500. Two batteries: 12.288 kWh ÷ 4.5 kW ≈ 2.7 h. One battery: 6.144 ÷ 4.5 ≈ 1.4 h. In Quiet mode (2 kW, ≤66 dB at 23 ft), two batteries take 12.288 ÷ 2 ≈ 6.1 h. These figures ignore losses.
  • One tank of gasoline. Anker rates the 10 L (2.64 gal) tank at about 17 kWh. That is 17 ÷ 12.288 ≈ 1.4 refills of the two-battery kit, or 17 ÷ 6.144 ≈ 2.8 refills of a one-battery kit.
  • Usable energy. The Solar Lab measured 87% efficiency and about 40 W idle draw on the E10. That gives 12.288 × 0.87 ≈ 10.7 kWh delivered, and 40 W × 24 h ≈ 0.96 kWh a day of overhead.
  • Your own 240 V standby generator. At the E10's 7,680 W limit at 240 V, 12.288 ÷ 7.68 ≈ 1.6 h. Anker says the E10 does not output power to the home while it charges or bypasses in this mode.
  • Price steps. The two-battery bundle is 9,399 dollars. The same parts bought separately cost 7,799 + 1,999 = 9,798 dollars, so the bundle saves 399. Going from one battery to two adds 9,399 − 7,399 = 2,000 dollars, which is the same as the B6000 add-on price on 2026-11-14.
Your situationKit
Whole house, nothing to switch by hand, fewest generator startsWhole house, fully automatic
Same automation, lower upfront cost, battery added laterAutomatic, smaller budget
Transfer switch and inlet box already installedExisting transfer switch owners
240 V standby generator with a two-wire start already installedAlready own a standby generator

{kit:kit-e10-two-battery-power-dock-generator} This is the pick for most homes. The Power Dock takes 200 A service and switches over in 20 ms or less. Twelve kWh in the batteries means the generator runs about every 12 kWh of use rather than every 6.

{kit:kit-e10-one-battery-power-dock-generator} Pick this for the same automatic setup at 2,000 dollars less. It holds half the energy, so the generator starts about twice as often. You can add a B6000 later.

{kit:kit-e10-inlet-box-generator} Pick this if your home already has a transfer switch and inlet box. Anker says the Smart Inlet Box 'fits a more manual backup strategy' and recommends the Power Dock with the Smart Generator 5500 for automatic whole-home backup.

{kit:kit-e10-two-battery-power-dock-own-standby} Pick this if you already have a 240 V standby generator with Two Wire or Utility Sensing control and no more than 24 kW surge. Anker added this support in its May 2026 firmware, and only for E10 + Power Dock.

Match the generator to the hub: voltage, start wire and link

A generator only refills the battery quickly, and only starts by itself, if its voltage and its start control match the hub. The E10 takes generator power three ways:

Generator connectionCharge rate into the E10Starts itself?
Smart Generator 5500 on its DC cable (power and communication)4,500 W Turbo, 4,000 W Eco, 2,000 W QuietYes, at a battery level you set
240 V generator on ACUp to 7,680 WOnly a standby model with Two Wire or Utility Sensing control, wired to the Power Dock
120 V generator on ACUp to 1,800 W; Anker says to keep continuous charging above 12 A under 3 hoursAnker: 'most portable models lack SOC-based or app-controlled auto-start'
  • 7,680 ÷ 1,800 ≈ 4.3: a 120 V generator refills the E10 about 4.3 times slower than a 240 V one. Against the Smart Generator's DC link, 4,500 ÷ 1,800 = 2.5 times slower.
  • The Smart Generator 5500's own AC outlets are 120 V only (one TT-30R and one NEMA 5-20R). Use its DC cable into the E10, not an AC cord.
  • The Power Dock works with any 240 V generator, with up to 24 kW of pass-through. Its circuits 1 and 2 are rated 100 A max / 80 A continuous when used for a generator.
  • For third-party generators, Anker asks for THD below 10% 'for stable charging'.
  • XDA's Joe Rice-Jones tested an Anker-installed E10 with Power Dock and Smart Generator. He wrote that the generator 'will be automatically started by the system when needed' and 'provides DC direct to the batteries'.

Not recommended

An E10 paired with a 120 V portable generator. It charges at 1,800 W, so two batteries take at least 12.288 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 6.8 h, against 2.7 h on the Smart Generator's DC cable. Anker also says most portables cannot start themselves. The E10 AC Generator Adapter in a Power Dock order. Anker lists it as 'Currently not compatible with Power Dock'. It is meant for E10 Standalone or Smart Inlet Box setups with a 240 V generator, up to 9,600 W at 240 V (40 A max).
